deep.reconstruction:
PART A (top; continues f.180). The setting: a function F(a,b) of two arcs and its derivative-type function f, with F(da,b) = da·f(b), the normalisation f(ρ) = λ/ρ (eq. 5 of f.180), and the ODE (7) df(b)/db = (ρk/λ) f(ρ−b), hence d f(ρ−b)/db = −(ρk/λ) f(b). Here ρ plays the role of a quadrant and the intent is plainly to show that the 'projection' function f is a sine, as in a functional-equation foundation of spherical trigonometry. On f.180 Gauss set B = f(ρ−b) + i f(b) and B' = f(ρ−b) − i f(b). He obtained dB = i(ρk/λ)B db, so B = (λ/ρ) e^{i b ρk/λ}, using B(0) = f(ρ) + i f(0) = λ/ρ; the condition f(0)=0 is implicit. This page draws the conclusions.
(i) Real and imaginary parts: f(b) = (λ/ρ) sin(ρk b/λ) and f(ρ−b) = (λ/ρ) cos(ρk b/λ).
(ii) Put b = ρ in the first and use f(ρ) = λ/ρ (my filling). This gives 1 = sin(ρ²k/λ).
(iii) Hence ρ²k/λ = π/2. Gauss tacitly takes the principal root; positivity or monotonicity of f on (0,ρ) would be needed to exclude π/2 + 2πn.
(iv) Therefore ρk/λ = π/(2ρ) and f(b) = (λ/ρ) sin(π b/(2ρ)). That is, f is the sine of the arc measured in units where a quadrant equals ρ.

PART B: 'Pentagramma mirificum'. The figure shows a spherical pentagon with sides 1,…,5 (the arcs). The dotted arcs carry the labels R−1,…,R−5, where R is a right angle, i.e. the complements of the parts. These form the outer star of five right triangles: Gauss's self-polar spherical pentagon, in which each vertex is the pole of the opposite side.

Right column: the five Napier relations cos1 = sin2·sin5, cos2 = sin3·sin1, cos3 = sin4·sin2, cos4 = sin5·sin3, cos5 = sin1·sin4. Each says that cos of a part equals the product of the sines of its two neighbours. These are Napier's rule 'sine of middle = product of cosines of opposite parts' applied to the complements R−i, with Napier cycle (1,3,5,2,4).

The tangent form of Napier's rule (sine of middle = product of tangents of adjacent parts) gives 1 = cos i · tg(i+2) · tg(i+3), indices mod 5:
- 1 = cos1·tg3·tg4
- 1 = cos2·tg4·tg5
- 1 = cos3·tg5·tg1
- 1 = cos4·tg1·tg2
- 1 = cos5·tg2·tg3
In the variables t_i = tan²(i) these are Gauss's well-known relations 1 + t1 = t3 t4, 1 + t2 = t4 t5, etc.

Left column, equations 8–12 (numbering continues the 1–7 of f.180): −d1 = d2·cos4 + d5·cos3, and cyclically. These are the logarithmic differentials of the cos-relations. My check: differentiating cos1 = sin2 sin5 gives −sin1 d1 = cos2 sin5 d2 + sin2 cos5 d5. Dividing by sin1 and using cos2 = sin1 sin3 and cos5 = sin1 sin4 gives −d1 = sin3 sin5 d2 + sin2 sin4 d5 = cos4 d2 + cos3 d5. Since the figure has only 2 degrees of freedom, the five linear relations have rank 3, and Gauss starts eliminating.
- Eliminating d5 between (8) and (12): substitute d5 = −d1 cos3 − d4 cos2 into (8). This gives d1 sin²3 = −d2 cos4 + d4 cos2 cos3.
- Eliminating d3 between (9) and (10): substitute d3 = −d4 cos1 − d2 cos5 into (9). This gives d2 sin²5 = −d1 cos4 + d4 cos1 cos5.
The page breaks off here. The next page (f.182) continues with the central projection: the plane pentagon has concurrent altitudes with equal products of segments, plus a Gaussian-integer parametrisation of its vertices.
errors: Top: the step sin(ρρk/λ)=1 ⇒ ρρk/λ = π/2 silently picks the principal solution; a justification (e.g. f>0 on (0,ρ), or ρ being the first zero of f(ρ−b)) is omitted. The condition f(0)=0, needed for B(0)=λ/ρ, is also implicit.

The elimination of d5 yielding d1 sin²3 = −d2 cos4 + d4 cos2 cos3 uses equations 8 and 12, not 8 and 11 as written/transcribed. Eq. 11 contains d3, which does not appear in the result. Either a slip by Gauss or a misreading of '12' (which Gauss writes like '1r').

As transcribed, the last two tangent identities '1 = cos4 tg1 tg3' and '1 = cos5 tg2 tg4' are false; they should read 1 = cos4·tg1·tg2 and 1 = cos5·tg2·tg3. Counterexample with tan² = (2, 3, 3/5, 5, 4/5): 1+t4 = 6 but t1 t3 = 1.2. Possibly a misreading of the handwritten digits, otherwise slips by Gauss.
The two eliminated equations themselves are correct.

results.what: Solution of the linear ODE system f' = c·g, g' = −c·f via B = g + i f to show that the projection function is f(b) = (λ/ρ) sin(πb/(2ρ)), with ρ = quadrant. This is part of an axiomatic/functional-equation derivation of spherical trigonometry.
results.modern_name: Characterisation of sine/cosine by the harmonic-oscillator ODE (functional-equation foundation of spherical trigonometry)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euler-era ODE technique); functional-equation derivations of trigonometric laws go back to d'Alembert/Legendre-era discussions

results.what: Pentagramma mirificum: self-polar spherical pentagon with the five Napier relations cos i = sin(i−1) sin(i+1) and 1 = cos i · tan(i+2) tan(i+3), equivalently 1 + tan²(i) = tan²(i+2)·tan²(i+3).
results.modern_name: Gauss's pentagramma mirificum (precursor of frieze patterns / cluster-algebra A2 recurrence of period 5)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass, published Werke III pp. ~481–490, 1866); the figure is also associated with Napier's rules; modern links via Coxeter's frieze patterns (1971)

results.what: Differential relations −d_i = cos(i+3) d(i+1) + cos(i+2) d(i−1) for deformations of the pentagram, and eliminations reducing to two independent differentials.
results.modern_name: Tangent space of the 2-parameter moduli of the pentagramma (linearisation of the Napier/pentagram relations)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Nachlass material on the pentagramma, printed in Werke III)

deep.surprise_reason: The pentagramma mirificum is famously Gauss's own and this sheet is evidently the source printed in Werke III; the pencil 'III 479' is the editor's reference. The top part is a routine ODE solution. Nothing here is new relative to what is credited to Gauss.

transcription_corrections: 'f(ξ − b)' should be f(ϱ − b); Gauss's ϱ is misread as ξ (cf. f.180).
'Die Elimination von d5 aus 8 und 11' — the computation requires 8 and 12; check whether the manuscript reads '12' (written like '1r').
In '= cos 3. tg5. tg1' the digit 3 is written over another numeral (a correction in the manuscript).

The last two tangent identities are transcribed as 'cos4 tg1.tg3' and 'cos5 tg2.tg4'; mathematically and by the cyclic pattern they should be cos4·tg1·tg2 and cos5·tg2·tg3. Re-check the digits in the image.
Dotted-arc labels 'R-1' … 'R-5' denote R − i, i.e. right angle minus part i (complements), not subtraction indices.
'III 479' is a later pencil editorial reference (Werke vol. III), not Gauss's text.
